items.title: Maria Schneider interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001
items.q: But they all — you know Scott Robinson, he’s into C melody saxophone and he’s into all sorts of old style things, but he also loves Sun Ra and he has such a wide world that’s coming — and I have that through all the different musicians.

ctx.x: Yeah. You know it’s something I started to realize about jazz, because I have to say I’m really disappointed in a lot of jazz I hear — not that I listen and say I’m disappointed — but I just lose interest pretty quickly. And I think that jazz at one time was music that, it just evolved. Later it was named jazz, and then everybody goes back and analyzes how it

came into being or whatever. But it was something that came up spontaneously from something very deep and cultural and human and personal and sociological, everything came together. And for me now, what happens is when people, say they’re writing music, they have this template of how music has been behind them. Like okay it’s jazz. That means it has a rhythm section, probably drumset, it means that there’s a bass line, it means that there is something comping, it means that there is a solo section, it means that…
that other thing. And then I codify it in notes, in little black dots and lines. To try to translate it. Does it make sense?
